Inferior alveolar nerve injury

A recent 60-person trial reported improved sensory measures versus sham after third-molar-related hypoesthesia; earlier evidence remains mixed.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

A recent 60-person trial reported improved sensory measures versus sham after third-molar-related hypoesthesia; earlier evidence remains mixed.

Summary of the Evidence

The exact inferior-alveolar category contains 47 unique titles: 17 RCT-tagged human reports, including one retracted publication, 12 other human reports, ten animal studies, and eight reviews or syntheses. The retracted report should be excluded from efficacy interpretation. The 2026 sham-controlled study is one recent trial cohort and does not resolve other injury causes. (Ma et al. 2026)

Human and clinical evidence

The randomized and nonrandomized studies cover paresthesia after third-molar extraction, implant surgery, and other oral procedures. In a 2026 double-blind trial, 60 adults with post-extraction hypoesthesia completed treatment. Direct PBM and laser acupuncture improved two-point discrimination and monofilament measures versus sham; improvements were largely maintained at day 60. The trial also administered mecobalamin to all participants, and its findings apply to the studied post-extraction population.

Animal evidence

Ten animal publications are indexed, including nine rat and one rabbit study. These models examine peripheral nerve repair but do not establish sensory recovery in human dental injuries.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No standalone in-vitro or ex-vivo study is indexed in the exact category.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The 2026 trial used an 808 nm near-infrared diode laser in continuous mode at 100 mW, with a 1 cm² beam and 9 J/cm² for 90 seconds per site. Treatment was delivered every other day for 15 sessions over 30 days. Mecobalamin was given to all groups. Other records use different wavelengths and schedules.

Interpretation

A 60-person sham-controlled trial reported improved sensory measures after third-molar-related hypoesthesia. This result applies to that selected post-extraction group. Other injury causes are less studied, and one related report is retracted. Future studies should stratify injury cause and severity, include appropriate controls, report co-interventions, and follow sensory function for longer periods.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow for sensory recovery after third-molar injury Very low for other nerve-injury causes

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

The category contains 47 titles, including 17 RCT-tagged reports, one of which is retracted, and 12 additional human reports. Most trials are small and address different injury causes. Further sham-controlled studies should replicate sensory outcomes and separate PBM from medication and spontaneous recovery.
